Lumen Labs' new e-reader charges from a sunny window

Sofia Marquez · October 21, 2026 · 48 comments

Lumen Labs, the small Dutch company behind last year's Lumen Slate, has announced an e-reader with a solar panel built into its back cover. The Lumen Leaf goes on sale in November for 189 euros, and the company says a few hours by a bright window each week is enough to keep it running without ever plugging it in.

The panel covers almost the whole rear of the device and sits under a matte, slightly textured glass. In the demonstration unit we held, it felt no different from the soft-touch plastic on most readers, and it added only a few grams compared with the Slate.

Inside is a 7.8-inch electronic paper screen with a resolution of 300 pixels per inch, a front light with adjustable warmth, and 32 gigabytes of storage. There are physical page-turn buttons along one edge, which the company says were the most requested feature from owners of its earlier models.

"Most people read in the evening, but their reader spends the day lying on a desk or a windowsill," said Joris van Dam, who leads product design at Lumen Labs. "We wanted that time to count for something. If you keep it face down near a window, you may simply never see the battery warning."

The company's own figures suggest that four hours of indirect daylight adds roughly a day of reading at medium brightness. Under a desk lamp the gain is far smaller, and on a cloudy week in northern Europe owners will still need the USB-C port now and then.

There are trade-offs. The Leaf has no waterproofing, which Lumen Labs says would have made the back panel thicker and less efficient. It also lacks the audiobook support found on several rivals, and its store is smaller, though it reads standard EPUB and PDF files and can receive documents by email.

Battery researchers we spoke to were cautiously positive. Small panels on consumer devices have a mixed record, mostly because people keep them in bags and drawers. An e-reader, which draws almost no power except when the page changes, is one of the few gadgets where the arithmetic can work.

We will publish a full review once we have lived with the Leaf for a few weeks, including a test of how it fares through a dark December. Pre-orders open on the company's website today, with shipping across Europe planned for the second week of November.
